title: EUR 24,640 a year, and 46 cents a month
angle: A one-man workshop loses EUR 24,640 a year to looking for a page, and the tool that gives it back costs cents a month to run. Every cell regenerable from ramp/numbers.py.
endline: Don't trust the AI. Trust the manual.

marks.do: The workshop. Then the money, before anything about the product.
EUR 44,000 — say the arithmetic in four steps, slowly.
Cut it yourself. "That number is too kind to me." EUR 24,640.
The stopwatch table. Say "machine time" out loud.
LIVE. Stopwatch on the phone, next to the app.
Why the bill is small — the diagram.
Under 1% of a seat. THE Ramp slide.
5.5 working days. And 22 if his 20% is really 5%.
522 M hours — then come back to "five people in the average shop".

notes: Say it, then two seconds of silence.
Then: "A friend of mine opened a motorcycle workshop in Germany a few years ago. He's a good mechanic. And about a fifth of his working time, he isn't fixing bikes. He's looking for a page."
Every time you quote a figure, say *measured*, *assumed*, or *his*. Doing that four or five times is the entire tone of this pitch.

slides.title: EUR 44,000
slides.line: Per mechanic. Per year. Say the arithmetic out loud, slowly, in four steps.
rows: a full-time self-employed German craftsman works
notes: *Do not editorialise the number.* Say the arithmetic in four steps: hours, share, rate, product. If you explain why it's big, it gets smaller. Let it sit.
The thing not to say: "the market for workshop software". Not yet. One man, one number.
Never say EUR 44,000 without immediately taking the deductions down to EUR 24,640 — that is the very next slide, and it is the most important one in the deck.

400 h × EUR 110/h — the gross, un-deducted figure. Never say it without the next slide.

slides.label: …and honestly,
slides.sub: Minus *30%* for recovery — he still has to read the page. Minus another *20%* for utilisation — an hour is only money if there's a bike waiting. *That's the number I'd sign for.*
notes: *This is the most important slide in the deck.* Every pitch in the room will show the previous slide. Almost none will show this one.
Say the words ~that number is too kind to me.~ Cutting your own headline in half on stage buys you every number after it.

The US version of the same arithmetic is $56,000 gross, $31,360 after the same deductions. ramp/numbers.md §7(b) runs the whole grid — at 30% recovery and 50% utilisation, the hostile corner, it is EUR 6,600 a year and the seat still pays back in 20 working days.

slides.title: Why the bill is small

Retrieval itself is free: BM25 in process, no embeddings, no vector database. Do not go further into architecture than this slide.

slides.note: *This is the Ramp slide.* "The AI line item is under one percent of the price of the seat" is the sentence a finance audience remembers.
notes: EUR 49 is what we would charge, and be straight that nobody has paid it yet.

What we will *not* do is charge per question: our cost is $0.00038 an ask, metering that costs more to bill than to serve — and the moment you meter it he rations it, and a tool you ration doesn't get the 400 hours back.
The expensive step — reading a manual end to end, $0.095 — happens once per manual, not once per question, and every shop that ever opens that bike shares it.

groups.label: All nine, global
items: ElevenLabs voice is never "live" — "built, one key away". The live voice is Deepgram.
The 3D backdrop is a technical grid. No panorama, no photographic workshop scene.
Dropbox folder sync and Climate Fit are "built, deploying", not deployed.
Never call 13,537 "manuals" — distinct fetchable PDFs is 14,770.
Never call 4,081 and 1,489 the same number.
There is no checkout. "Live prices", never "buy".
